extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and principles for construing patent claim terms (role of claims vs specification, intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence, means-plus-function rules, prosecution history, dictionaries, expert testimony, and standards of review). Applicable to litigation, prosecution, and appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function treatment avoided by sufficient structure recitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitation in patent claim reciting 'internal steel baffles extending inwardly from steel shell walls' recited sufficient structure to avoid means-plus-function treatment. 35 U.S.C.A. §112, par. 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim identifies particular structure (here 'internal steel baffles') rather than using a pure functional placeholder, §112, para. 6 (means-plus-function) does not apply. The absence of the word 'means' creates a rebuttable presumption that §112, para. 6 does not apply. Means-plus-function applies only to purely functional limitations that do not provide the structure performing the function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define the invention and right to exclude
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a bedrock principle of patent law that 'claims of patent define invention to which patentee is entitled the right to exclude.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are the primary measure of the patentee's rights; courts must look to the claim language to determine what the applicant regarded as the invention. Do not rewrite claims to include elements not in their plain import except according to established claim-construction tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary and customary meaning to person of skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of patent claim are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning, i.e., meaning that term would have to person of ordinary skill in the art in question on effective filing date of patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim terms as a person of ordinary skill in the art would at the time of the invention; this objective baseline governs claim interpretation unless patentee's lexicography or disavowal dictates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual reading by person of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Person of ordinary skill in the art, through whose eyes patent claim is construed, is deemed to read claim term not only in context of particular claim in which disputed term appears, but in context of entire patent, including specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim terms must be read in the full context of the patent (claims, specification) to capture how a skilled artisan would understand them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent usage across claims illuminates meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Because claim terms are normally used consistently throughout patent, usage of term in one claim can often illuminate meaning of same term in other claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare usage of a term across the claims; definitions or nuance in one claim can inform interpretation in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of dependent patent claim that adds particular limitation gives rise to presumption that limitation in question is not present in independent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a dependent claim narrows an independent claim by adding a limitation, presume that limitation was not intended to be included in the independent claim absent contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims read in view of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims must be read in view of specification, of which they are part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification is part of the intrinsic evidence and must be consulted when construing claim language; claims are not interpreted in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification as single best guide
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent specification is always highly relevant to claim construction analysis; it is single best guide to meaning of disputed term, and is usually dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give primary weight to the specification when interpreting claim terms; where the specification clearly indicates a meaning, that guidance will often control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's lexicography controls when present
rubrics_metrics.description: When patent specification reveals special definition given to claim term by patentee that differs from meaning it would otherwise possess, inventor’s lexicography governs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee explicitly defines a term in the specification, adopt that meaning even if it departs from the term's ordinary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disavowal limits claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Where patent specification reveals intentional disclaimer, or disavowal, of claim scope by inventor, such revealed intention is dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear and unambiguous disavowal or disclaimer in the specification or prosecution history will limit claim scope accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history as intrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Prosecution history' consists of complete record of proceedings before Patent and Trademark Office and includes prior art cited during examination of patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prosecution history to understand how the inventor and PTO interpreted terms and whether the inventor limited claims during prosecution; treat it as part of the intrinsic record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history informs claim meaning by showing patentee's understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history can often inform meaning of patent claim language by demonstrating how inventor understood invention and whether inventor limited invention in course of prosecution, making claim scope narrower than it would otherwise be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine arguments, amendments, and cited art in prosecution history for evidence of limiting statements or disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence secondary to intrinsic record
rubrics_metrics.description: Although extrinsic evidence can shed useful light on relevant art, it is less significant than intrinsic record in determining legally operative meaning of patent claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, prosecution history); use extrinsic evidence only to aid understanding, not to override intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries as useful extrinsic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries, though extrinsic evidence, are among tools that can assist patent-construing court in determining meaning of particular terminology to those of skill in the art of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult dictionaries with caution and in context; they can be informative about ordinary meanings but cannot contradict clear intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony can be helpful but limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence in form of expert testimony can be useful to patent-construing court for a variety of purposes, such as to provide background on technology at issue, to explain how invention works, to ensure that court’s understanding of technical aspects of patent is consistent with that of person of skill in the art, or to establish that particular term in patent or prior art has particular meaning in pertinent field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expert testimony to provide technical context and explain how a skilled artisan would view terms, but weigh such testimony against intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject conclusory unsupported expert assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusory, unsupported assertions by experts as to definition of patent claim term are not useful to construing court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit expert evidence when well-founded; disregard unsupported or conclusory opinions that lack record support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discount expert testimony that conflicts with intrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Court, when construing patent, should discount any expert testimony that is clearly at odds with claim construction mandated by claims themselves, written description, and prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic evidence (claims/specification/prosecution) controls; extrinsic expert opinions conflicting with it carry little weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence must be considered in context of intrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence may be useful to construing court, but it is unlikely to result in reliable interpretation of patent claim scope unless considered in context of intrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interpret extrinsic evidence in isolation; always test it against the intrinsic record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may use extrinsic evidence in its discretion to educate itself
rubrics_metrics.description: It is permissible for patent-construing court, in its sound discretion, to admit and use extrinsic evidence; such evidence can help educate court regarding field of invention and can help court determine what person of ordinary skill in the art would understand claim terms to mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit extrinsic materials (textbooks, treatises, expert reports) when they genuinely illuminate the field and the skilled artisan's understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictionaries useful but focus on skilled artisan's understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Although dictionaries or comparable sources are often useful to assist in understanding commonly understood meaning of patent claim terms, construing court’s focus remains on understanding how person of ordinary skill in the art would understand claim terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give dictionaries weight only insofar as they reflect the skilled artisan's understanding at the relevant time; do not substitute them for intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: No required formula or sequence for claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no magic formula or catechism for conducting patent claim construction; court is not barred from considering any particular sources or required to analyze sources in any specific sequence, so long as those sources are not used to contradict claim meaning that is unambiguous in light of intrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexibility is permitted in the order and sources consulted for claim construction, but intrinsic evidence governs when it is unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should not be limited to preferred embodiment absent clear intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal steel 'baffles,' called for in patent for vandalism-resistant wall panels, were not limited to non-perpendicular, projectile-deflecting structures disclosed in preferred embodiment; specification did not require that internal structures always be capable of performing that function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not import limitations from the preferred embodiment into claim scope unless the specification or prosecution history clearly requires such limitation (lexicography or disavowal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives stated in specification do not automatically limit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact that patent asserts that invention achieves several objectives does not require that each claim be construed as limited to structures that are capable of achieving all those objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reading every stated objective of the invention as a claim limitation; only adopt limitations when supported by the intrinsic record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting construction to preserve validity is a last resort
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of patent construction maxim, that claims should be so construed, if possible, as to sustain their validity, is limited to cases in which court concludes, after applying all available tools of claim construction, that claim is still ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when, after exhausting intrinsic-and-appropriate-extrinsic analysis, a claim remains ambiguous may a court consider a construction that favors validity; do not construe claims to save validity when intrinsic evidence is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of the word 'means' creates rebuttable presumption against §112, para. 6
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of the term 'means' in a claim limitation creates a rebuttable presumption that §112, paragraph 6 (means-plus-function) does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the presumption that §112, para. 6 is inapplicable when 'means' is not used; the presumption can be rebutted by showing that the claim term fails to recite sufficiently definite structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function applies only to purely functional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function claiming applies only to purely functional limitations that do not provide the structure that performs the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim language supplies structure (even if the structure has functional connotations), do not treat it as a means-plus-function limitation; compare to case law examples (e.g., 'compressed spring' vs general 'means').

rubrics_metrics.name: Contested view—underlying factual findings deserve deference (Rule 52(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsidiary factual determinations underlying claim construction (e.g., level of ordinary skill, state of the art, meaning of terms to skilled artisan) are inherently factual and should be reviewed for clear error under Rule 52(a), rather than de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a position articulated in the opinion's discussion of standards of review: district court factfinding (expert disputes, technical background) typically merits deference; appellate courts should accept district courts' factual findings unless clearly erroneous. Note: this view reflects disagreement among judges and represents the argument for deference to trial-court factfinding.
